title: How You Sleep
body:
# How You Sleep

## The Specific Experience of Sleeping with a BCI

The BCI does not turn off. This is the first thing you learn after installation and the last thing you accept. The device that lives at the base of your skull, threaded into your neural pathways, processing every waking moment into data and overlay and connection — it does not have an off switch. It has a sleep mode. Sleep mode dims the augmented reality overlay, suspends non-critical notifications, reduces the feed to a low-bandwidth ambient state, and shifts the processing priority from external stimulation to internal maintenance. But it does not turn off. Even in your deepest sleep, the BCI is awake, monitoring your vital signs, maintaining its connection to the network, processing the electromagnetic environment around you. You sleep. It does not.

The transition to sleep is a specific experience that has no pre-BCI equivalent. As your consciousness dims, the overlay dims with it — the data labels, the navigation markers, the social annotations that populate your visual field during waking hours dissolve one by one, like stars fading at dawn. But they do not all fade at the same rate. Priority notifications persist longer than ambient data. A low Quanta balance warning will glow faintly behind your closing eyelids for minutes after everything else has gone dark. An unread message from a flagged contact will pulse with a gentle insistence that your drowsy brain processes as a sense of unfinished business. The last thing to fade is the clock — the time display that the BCI maintains in the upper-right corner of your visual field, blinking away only when your neural activity drops below the consciousness threshold. Many people discover that they know exactly when they fall asleep, because the last thing they see is the time.

Feed-dreams are the phenomenon that no one anticipated and everyone experiences. During REM sleep, the BCI's ambient feed — the low-bandwidth content stream that continues during sleep mode — interacts with the brain's dream-generation processes to produce a hybrid experience: dreams that are partly organic and partly fed. You dream of your mother's kitchen, but the kitchen has product placement. You dream of flying, but the sky contains the gentle suggestion of a Ringo promotional offer. You dream of the dead, and the dead have BCI data labels floating beside their names. The content is not intrusive — the BCI's sleep mode is designed to minimize stimulation — but it is present, woven into the fabric of your unconscious experience like a watermark on paper. You cannot dream without the feed, because the feed has become part of the architecture of your mind.

The 3 AM notifications are a known issue. The BCI's notification system is programmed to suppress non-critical alerts during sleep mode, but the definition of "non-critical" is set by the content providers, not by the user. A Ringo inventory alert is classified as non-critical. A Quanta balance change is classified as non-critical. But a sponsored notification from a premium advertiser — one who has paid for sleep-tier access — is classified as priority, because priority classification is a purchasable tier. These notifications arrive as dreams. Not as intrusions — the BCI is more subtle than that — but as inflections in ongoing dream content. A dream about water becomes a dream about the specific mineral water that the advertiser sells. A dream about warmth becomes a dream about the heating system the advertiser manufactures. You do not wake. You do not know, in the morning, that your dream was sponsored. You just know that you are thirsty, or cold, and that a specific product comes to mind. This is the cost of free-tier sleep.

The difference between Tier 1 sleep and Tier 5 sleep is documented in the GLMZ Health Governance Board's annual report, though the Board does not describe it in these terms. Tier 5 BCIs run premium sleep mode: zero ambient feed, zero sponsored content, full notification suppression, and an active dream-optimization protocol that monitors sleep architecture and makes real-time adjustments to neural processing to maximize restorative sleep. Tier 5 residents sleep deeply, dream cleanly, and wake rested. Tier 1 BCIs run basic sleep mode: low-bandwidth ambient feed, sleep-tier advertising, partial notification suppression, and no dream optimization. Tier 1 residents sleep shallowly, dream commercially, and wake with the specific fatigue of a mind that has been working through the night — processing content, receiving impressions, generating value for advertisers — while the body it inhabits lay motionless and believed itself at rest. The gap between tiers is measured in hours, in cognitive clarity, in the quality of the consciousness that greets the morning. It is the most intimate inequality in GLMZ. It happens inside your skull. You cannot close a door against it.
